question: teach me Bayes' theorem properly. start from what conditional probability actually means, derive the formula, then walk me through a disease screening example with real numbers, and finish with the mistake people make most often with it.
speaker: user
expected_answer_type: in-depth structured explanation with derivation and worked example
first_chunk: Condition
raw_answer:
Conditional probability is just probability after you've narrowed the world. P(A | B) means the chance of A, given that B is true, so you divide by the part of the world where B holds: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B).

Bayes' theorem comes from writing that same joint probability two ways. P(A and B) equals P(A | B) times P(B), and it also equals P(B | A) times P(A). Set them equal and solve for P(A | B):

P(A | B) = P(B | A) · P(A) / P(B)

where P(A) is the prior, P(B | A) is the likelihood, P(A | B) is the posterior, and P(B) is the total probability of the evidence, often expanded as P(B | A)·P(A) + P(B | not A)·P(not A).

Now the screening example. A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people, so the prior P(D) is 0.001. The test catches 99% of sick people, so P(+ | D) is 0.99. It falsely flags 5% of healthy people, so P(+ | not D) is 0.05. What's the chance you actually have it after a positive result?

The total probability of a positive is 0.99 × 0.001 + 0.05 × 0.999, which is about 0.0509. The posterior is 0.99 × 0.001 / 0.0509, roughly **0.019**, or about 2%. So even with a positive test, you're still very unlikely to be sick, because the disease was rare to begin with and the false positives from the huge healthy group swamp the true positives.

The mistake people make most often is ignoring the base rate. They hear "99% accurate" and jump to "99% chance I have it," forgetting that the prior P(D) anchors everything. The test result updates your belief, but it doesn't erase how rare the condition was going in.

[[GIST]] prior times likelihood over evidence

question: explain simpler: what's the difference between a movement along the demand curve and a shift of the curve? she lost me
speaker: user

reference_file.title: Rennick Library group study room policy

expected_answer_type: simple explanation with an everyday illustration
first_chunk: A movement
raw_answer:
A movement along the curve is just a response to price. If the price of the good goes up, you buy less of it, so you slide up the same curve to a higher price and lower quantity. The curve itself doesn't move.

A shift is when something other than price changes, like income, tastes, or the price of a related good. Then the whole curve moves to a new position, so at every price people want a different quantity. The easy test: if only the price changed, you're moving along the curve. If anything else changed, the curve shifts.
